title: Options Playbook
html:
What we trade: buying calls (betting up) and buying puts (betting down), then selling to close. No selling options to open, no spreads — for now. Why this is the right place to start: the most you can lose on a bought option is what you paid for it. The honest catch: most bought options lose money or expire worthless, because time decay works against you every day. The edge has to come from good timing — which is where the charts come in.

The basics

  • One contract = 100 shares. An option quoted at $2.50 costs $250.
  • Calls gain when the stock rises above the strike; puts gain when it falls below.
  • Expiration: the option is worth nothing after this date if it's out of the money.
  • Strike choice: at-the-money or slightly in-the-money options (delta ~0.50–0.65) move more like the stock. Cheap far out-of-the-money options are lottery tickets.

The Greeks in one line each

GreekPlain English
DeltaHow much the option moves per $1 move in the stock (0.50 = $0.50)
ThetaHow much value the option loses each day just from time passing
VegaHow much it gains or loses when expected volatility (IV) changes
GammaHow fast delta changes — high near expiration, which makes short-dated options jumpy

Turning a chart setup into a trade

  1. Setup from the chart — e.g., SPY pulls back to the $740–745 Fib cluster and bounces.
  2. Direction — bounce from support → call; rejection at resistance → put.
  3. Expiration — give the trade time: aim for 30–60 days out so theta doesn't eat you alive. Avoid same-day (0DTE) options while learning.
  4. Strike — near the money (delta ~0.50–0.65).
  5. Exit plan before entry — target = next Fib level; stop = if the stock closes beyond the level that made the setup valid (or the option loses 40–50%).
  6. Check the calendar — before earnings, options are expensive and usually drop sharply right after (IV crush), even if you guessed direction right.
  • Max risk per trade: TBD % of the account (pros often use 1–5%)
  • Max total in open options at once: TBD
  • No buying options the day before earnings unless it's a deliberate earnings bet
  • Every trade logged in Trade Log before and after
  • Liquidity check: open interest in the hundreds or more, bid-ask spread a few cents, not dimes

Webull cash-account notes

  • Options approval is required on the account before trading options.
  • In a cash account, option trades settle the next business day (T+1); you can only trade with settled cash, which avoids pattern-day-trader rules but limits how fast money can be reused.
  • Claude does not place, change or cancel trades. All orders are yours.
